title: How an education product should write an about page
metaTitle: Education product about page: who writes the lessons
excerpt: Name who writes the lessons and why a teacher or parent should trust them. Skip the origin myth unless it changes the decision to start.
alt: Five people working on laptops around a wooden table, the group an about page has to turn into named roles.
caption: Five people working on laptops around a wooden table. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Who should an education about page name?
faqs.answer: The people who edit the lessons, design the practice, build the product, and answer a teacher when a class goes wrong. Give each person a job, not a trait. Do not invent advisors who review nothing.

faqs.question: When does a founder story belong?
faqs.answer: When it predicts a product decision, such as a short practice or a teacher view that lists who is stuck. A garage, a mascot child, or a memoir before those facts delays the check the buyer came to make.

faqs.question: What should you show instead of stock students?
faqs.answer: The real editors and the lesson they stand behind, or the product frame with fictional names. Children's faces need a higher permission bar. When you are unsure, show the lesson, not a child.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
An education product about page is proof that people stand behind the lessons. Name who does the work, and why a teacher or a parent with little time should care. Skip the origin myth unless it changes the decision to start a class or a trial.

They are not shopping for a personality. They are checking whether a careful person is responsible for what a child will see, and whether that person understands a classroom or a weeknight.

## Who stands behind the lessons

Open with the roles, not the childhood of the founder. Who writes or edits the lessons. Who designs the practice. Who builds the product. Who answers a teacher when a class goes wrong on a Tuesday. A parent should know there is a name. A teacher should know whether the name has been in a room with students, if you claim that, and you should claim it only when it is true.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks you to be clear about who created the page and why it exists. An about page that says "we are a team of dreamers" fails. An about page that names the work, the limit, and the person who owns the content succeeds. Dreamers are not an accountability structure.

Small is allowed. A small product company that can say "these two people edit every lesson" is often more believable than a stock photo of a large office. Do not rent a crowd. Do not invent advisors. If an advisor reviews nothing, they do not belong in the first screen of trust.

Give each published person a job a buyer can use. "Edits the reading lessons and writes the teacher notes." "Builds the class view so a teacher can see who is stuck." Traits such as passionate, lifelong learner, and kid-at-heart are shared by every weak education site. Jobs are checkable. The work on the rest of the site should match them.

## Why a teacher or a parent should care

Translate the jobs into the buyer's risk. A parent is risking a child's time and a bit of money, and sometimes a feeling of having failed if the app is a mess. A teacher is risking a period and their reputation with the class. The about page should say how you behave when that risk shows up.

State the standards you actually hold. Lessons that can be finished in the time you advertise. Language a tired adult can read. No public shaming, if that is a real rule. A trial that is the real product. Errors in the content get fixed in the open, not argued away. These standards are more persuasive than a paragraph about changing the world.

Say who you are not for. Families who want a tutor on call. Districts that need a custom curriculum by August if you cannot staff it. Teachers who need every subject. A refusal saves the trial for people you can help. It also signals that a human made a choice, which is the feeling an about page is supposed to create.

Hanabi's own standard, clarity over complexity, is a useful pattern for the sentence you put here. Yours might be: the lesson comes before the badge, and a class can start without a sales process. Whatever it is, the product and the homepage have to obey it. If the homepage is a dashboard of streaks and the about page talks about calm practice, a careful buyer will believe the dashboard.

One link to the offer is enough. The about page is not the services page and not the pricing page. Point to them when the reader asks what to buy. Do not paste them underneath a founder letter.

## Origin stories that do not help

An origin earns its place when it predicts the product. You taught the grade you are building for, and you got tired of worksheet nights, so the practice is short and the teacher view is a list of who is stuck. You learned to read late, so the product never uses a timer that panics a child. Those sentences change the hire, or the trial.

An origin does not earn its place when it is scenery. A garage. A favorite teacher with no connection to the lesson design. A child of your own used as a mascot. Parents are wary of their children becoming someone else's anecdote. If a family story is the reason, tell the decision it caused, and leave the rest of the family off the page.

Put any origin after the standards. Lead with who is responsible for the lesson a student will see tonight. A long letter from the founder before that fact is a delay. This reader has little time. They opened About because the homepage was interesting and they wanted a human check, not because they wanted a memoir.

Do not publish a founding year, a headcount, or a user count unless it is true and you are willing to update it. Stale scale is a kind of myth. Silence plus a clear lesson is finer. You do not need to look like a district vendor to be trusted with a class. You need the lesson to be honest and the people to be real.

## How the work is made

A short account of how a lesson ships is better than a values list. Who drafts it. Who checks it. What you do when a teacher reports a wrong answer. How fast that fix lands, in a window you have actually kept. This is the "how" a skeptical buyer wanted when they clicked About.

Mention the tools only if they change that story. A curriculum doc they can read. A design file in Figma. A production app that matches the marketing frames. Hanabi uses Figma for structure and ships interfaces in Next.js, React, and TypeScript when the engagement includes the build. Your about page should name your true habit, not a borrowed stack. The habit the buyer cares about is review, not the framework.

If teachers or parents help you test, say what they are asked to do and what you changed because of it. "We listen to our community" is not a method. "A teacher in the pilot told us the class view took too many taps, so the stuck-student list is now the first screen" is a method. Publish that only when it happened.

Privacy belongs here in one sentence and a link, not as the whole page. Who can see a child's work. What you do not sell. Where the longer policy lives. A parent should not have to finish a manifesto to find this. A teacher should not have to forward a riddle to an administrator.

## A face, a method, a boundary

If you show photographs, show the real people in the jobs you named. A portrait with a job line. Not a stock classroom. Not a child who is not a user you have permission to show. Children's faces are a high bar. When in doubt, show the lesson, not the child. The learning moment can carry the emotion without borrowing a stranger's kid.

Connect one portrait to one artifact. The editor, and a lesson they stand behind. The designer, and the class view. The about page fails when the faces and the product could be from different companies. Put them in the same scroll and use the same words the product uses.

Keep the boundary on the page. You are not a school. You are not a doctor. You are not a guarantee of a grade. Say the role in one line so the warmth does not overclaim. Warmth without a boundary is how education brands become creepy or careless. You can be kind and precise in the same paragraph.

The title can be plain and specific. [Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) prefers titles that describe the page and are not a pile of slogans. "About" plus nothing else wastes the tab. A title that says who makes the lessons, and for whom, is enough. The heading on the page can be the human sentence.

## Starting from this page

End with the same action as the rest of the site. Start a class, or start a trial. One line on what they need. The about page is often the last check before a parent enters an email or a teacher pastes a link into a staff chat. Do not make the button a new idea. Do not ask them to "join the movement."

If the page is still a letter about a dream, cut the letter until the jobs remain. Then put one lesson beside the people who made it. If the lesson and the people disagree, fix the lesson or fix the sentences. Do not add another value to the list.

When you want that page held to a standard you can see in finished work, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). Notice how a project states a decision without a myth. Your about page can do the same: a person, a method, a limit, and a way to begin.

Proof is the next piece, because a role and a portrait are not yet a classroom story. [Proof pages for an education product](/blog/proof-pages-for-an-education-product) should show the constraint, the decision, and the learning moment. The about page can point to one of them. It should not try to be all of them.
